title: Customer Success QBR — Northwind
description: Quarterly business review. Adoption, the rate-limit incident, and renewal.
transcript: Peter, Grace — thanks for joining. I know we're overdue for this one.
It's been a busy quarter on our side too. No complaints.
I've got Tom here as well since renewal comes up in this conversation.
I want to structure this as adoption first, then the incident, then renewal. But if the incident is front of mind we can start there.
Let's do adoption first. The incident matters but I don't want it to dominate.
Appreciated. So — you're at three hundred and twelve active users, up from two hundred and forty at the last review.
That growth is almost entirely the operations team. They went from a pilot to full rollout in about six weeks.
Honestly, one manager. She started sharing meeting summaries in the team channel and people asked how she was doing it.
That's the best kind of adoption. It's very hard to manufacture.
We've tried to manufacture it elsewhere and it doesn't work the same way.
Engineering, mostly. They're sceptical of anything that records them.
That's common. Is it a privacy concern or a signal-to-noise one?
Both, but mostly signal-to-noise. Their standups are five minutes and the summary is longer than the meeting.
That's fair criticism, and it's a real product gap. Short meetings summarise badly.
It's not a dealbreaker. It just means engineering won't be a growth area for you here.
Understood. I'd rather know that than chase it.
On usage — you're averaging about eleven hundred meetings a month, which is well within your tier.
What happens if operations doubles again?
You'd want a conversation before that, and Tom would need to be in it.
There's headroom in the current tier but not that much. Better to plan it than trip over it.
Right. The incident. I want to go through what happened rather than just apologise.
On the Tuesday, a configuration change intended for trial accounts applied to all accounts. It reduced your API rate limit by ninety percent for forty minutes.
We noticed because our integration started failing. It took us about fifteen minutes to work out it wasn't our side.
That's the part I'm sorriest about. You spent fifteen minutes debugging our problem.
It happens. What I'd want is to hear about it from you rather than find it ourselves.
That's the actual complaint, if I'm honest. Not the outage — the notification.
That's a fair complaint and I don't have a good answer for it.
We don't currently have a way to proactively notify affected accounts during an incident. We found out you were affected because you told us.
It is backwards. I'll take that back internally as a specific ask rather than general feedback.
Would a status page have helped, or do you want direct contact?
A status page helps but only if we think to look. An email to the technical contact would have saved the fifteen minutes.
That's clear enough to act on. Thank you.
What's the fix on your side so it doesn't recur?
Config changes are moving behind review with a staged rollout. I can share the summary of the postmortem if that's useful.
It would be. Our security team will ask.
Was there any commercial impact? I'd rather ask directly.
Not really. It was forty minutes in the middle of our afternoon and the queue caught up.
If it had been month-end close it would be a different conversation.
Can I move us to renewal, or is there more on the incident?
You're up in four months. I'm not going to do a hard sell today — I mainly want to know what would make it an easy yes.
Incident communication, which we've covered. And a serious answer on SSO.
Okta. We're consolidating everything onto it by the end of the year.
That's supported on the enterprise tier.
Then it's a configuration exercise, not a purchase. Elena, can we get that scheduled?
Yes. It's about a two-hour session with someone from your identity team.
I can arrange that. Better before the end of the quarter.
The other thing — and this is smaller — is user management. Removing a leaver takes three clicks in three places.
That's a real gap. Bulk deprovisioning is on the roadmap but I won't pretend it's imminent.
It would, and it's the same project. I'll find out where it actually sits and come back with a date or an honest 'not this year'.
I'd take an honest 'not this year' over a vague yes.
Anything else that would make renewal harder?
Pricing, potentially. We've heard rumours of a model change.
There is one coming, and I'd rather you heard the shape of it from me than from a rumour.
Enterprise moves to usage-based. Existing contracts are grandfathered for two quarters and there's sixty days' notice before anything changes.
Would we be better or worse off?
I don't have your numbers modelled yet. I'd rather come back with a real figure than guess on a call.
Let me recap so nothing gets lost. I'm sending the postmortem summary this week, and times for the SSO session.
I'm taking the incident notification gap back internally as a specific ask, and finding out where SCIM actually sits.
And I'm modelling Northwind under usage-based pricing, back to you in two weeks.
I'll get our identity team to respond on SSO timing.
That's a useful session. Thanks both.

summary.overview: Northwind has grown to 312 active users from 240, driven almost entirely by organic adoption in the operations team; engineering has not adopted and likely will not, because short standups summarise poorly. The rate-limit incident was discussed frankly, and the substantive complaint was not the outage but the absence of proactive notification — Northwind discovered it themselves and spent fifteen minutes debugging someone else's problem. Renewal in four months hinges on incident communication and a concrete answer on Okta SSO, which is already available on their tier. SCIM for bulk deprovisioning is wanted but Elena committed to an honest date or an honest no.
summary.gist: Healthy adoption, renewal turns on incident comms and SSO; notification gap is the real complaint.

bullets: 312 active users, up from 240 at the last review.
Growth is almost entirely operations, seeded by one manager sharing summaries in a team channel.
~1,100 meetings/month — within tier, but a further doubling needs a conversation first.
Engineering is sceptical: partly privacy, mostly signal-to-noise.
Five-minute standups produce summaries longer than the meeting — acknowledged as a real product gap.
Elena chose not to chase engineering rather than pretend it is winnable.
Northwind discovered the incident themselves and spent ~15 minutes debugging our problem.
There is currently no mechanism to notify affected accounts during an incident.
A status page helps only if you think to look; an email to the technical contact is what was wanted.
Okta SSO is available on their existing tier — a configuration exercise, not a purchase.
Two-hour session needed with Northwind's identity team, ideally before quarter end.
Removing a leaver takes three clicks in three places; SCIM would solve it but has no committed date.
Usage-based enterprise pricing disclosed proactively rather than left to rumour.
Grandfathering for two quarters and sixty days' notice both stated explicitly.
Northwind's own position to be modelled and returned within two weeks.

action_items.text: Send Northwind the incident postmortem summary
Send proposed times for the Okta SSO configuration session
Raise proactive incident notification for affected accounts as a product ask
Find out where SCIM sits and return with a date or an honest 'not this year'
Model Northwind's position under usage-based pricing
Arrange Northwind identity team availability for SSO
Review whether short meetings should summarise differently

soundbites.title: The real complaint: notification, not the outage
